This is wishful thinking. AI system must align with human values. Yeah, right.

First of all, we cannot agree what those values are.

The bigger problem is that this is architecturally not possible. LLMs are next word predictors, they are not self aware, they are not thinking, they have no empathy. You can think of this as water going down a very complex path, where next word prediction can take you anywhere.

If you are to ask LLM how to make your soup taste better, most of the times it will tell you something like "Add more salt" or whatever. That is generally higher probability. But LLMs read the whole internet as training. Lower probability, but still possible is "you should kill yourself as you are a bad cook". To LLM, those two are equivalent. One is just more probable than the other, but both will happen.

Last 2 years or so, we have been adding constraint after constraint to fix this (do not tell people to put glue on pizza, etc.), but you cannot possibly predict every possible failure mode. 
The only way out of this is to make an explicit law that if you set up AI system, you click the button, it causes damage, you are on the hook, legally. You do not know how to use them to avoid this? Do not use them. 

I do not see another option/

I note the caption under the leading photo includes "Traditionally, oil exporting countries, like Saudi Arabia and the United States, have held the power, ..."

The notion that the U.S. is an "oil exporting country" is somewhat misleading, as, unqualified, it implies we are a net exporter of crude oil, but in fact we are a net IMPORTER of crude oil. (Only a net exporter of petroleum products, and the accounting for those is somewhat dubious).

Referring to the summary at eia.gov
https://www.eia.gov/dnav/pet/pet_sum_sndw_dcus_nus_4.htm

We're currently producing 13.8 million barrels per day (bpd), yet our refineries are using 17.5 million bpd of crude and other inputs. Scrolling down the summary, one finds we're importing 6.5 million bpd of crude, while exporting about 4 million bpd of crude, i.e. we HAVE TO IMPORT 2.5 million bpd of crude to keep out refineries running.

Looking at exports, we find 2 million bpd of propane, but most of that is derived from natural gas liquids plants, NOT from refineries processing crude oil. Also 150,000 bpd of (corn) ethanol, which is decidedly NOT from an oil refinery/oil well. Hidden in the motor gasoline is a certain amount of alkylates, derived from propanes/butanes - again much of that from natural gas liquids plants. Add in refinery gains (increase in volume due to refining), and the export accounting dubiousness is complete.

We are a net importer of crude oil! (With low stockpiles).

comments.name: Heather DCruz
comments.body: I’m Australian. We have compulsory voting. This means everyone is expected to show up at a polling booth or in other legal ways, demonstrate they have collected a ballot. They can do whatever they like with their ballot once they receive it, including putting a blank ballot into the secure box. Our federal (and state) elections are always held on Saturdays, although early voting is available as are mail ballots. We have independent electoral commissions at federal and state levels. These independent commissions attend to the drawing of electoral districts depending on population distribution (numbers only, not any other characteristics) so that there are relatively even numbers in each electorate. Australia invented the secret ballot which early on was known as the Australian ballot. We also have what’s known as preferential voting which allows each voter to number in the order of their preference, their choice of candidates. We do have two major parties, but our system allows for minor parties and independents across the spectrum, so voters can give their first preference to someone of the very left, progressive party numbering down the list to the least preferred, or vice versa. Unfortunately, our more recent experiences are showing frightening tendencies of the influence of Donald Trump and MAGA policies as a far right extremist party is now suddenly gaining popularity. Some of it is arrogance:
Some authoritarians are like overly stern parents
who really believe "father knows best"
and that the people are children who need to be led.
But of course, the best way to lead is to lead by example.
But not every example makes sense
-- either to children or to the people.
So, the children (and the people) might drag their feet.

Other authoritarians (like many parents)
are simply selfish,
but the children (and the people) will usually see that
and will drag their feet even more or actively resist.
Coercion has limits.

Some of it is human nature:
Everybody wants to be liked.
Also, everybody wants to be remembered as good.

Some of it is practical:
A smart ruler knows that he heeds widespread support
to stay in power and to get people to do what he wants.
Coercion has limits, and smart authoritarians know this.

He also knows people will do more of the things he wants,
and do it better and more effectively,
if they think that what he wants is what they want.

Of course, people can be manipulated.
But as Abe Lincoln (or some other wise politician) said,
you can fool some of the people all of the time
and you can fool all of the people some of the time,
but you cannot fool all of the people all of the time.

However, many politicians fool themselves into  thinking
that they have widespread support when they really do not.

comments.body: Very sad to see another “Mexico is Dirty” article by the New York Times. Some factual corrections. First, Mexico City started sending the Mezquital Valley its untreated wastewater at the turn of the last century, under Porfirio Diaz. The system predates the Mexican Revolution. Diverting stormwater and wastewater did not start “quietly” in the 1970’s, as the article claims. It started with celebrations and pride in the completion of an impressive feat of engineering that would improve health and hygiene in Mexico City in 1901. This did not “transform it into the dumping ground for more than 20 million people.” When the system was built, Mexico City had around 400,000 people, which produced a lazy surface stream of wastewater for the production of hydro-electricity. Later, as the city grew exponentially, the amount of wastewater increased proportionally. This article does a very poor job of explaining the nuances of this complex system. The narrative of “Mexico is Dirty isn’t that Crazy” is much easier to write than an alternative perspective like: this is the world’s largest experiment in fixing our agricultural system’s broken relationship to nitrogen that is unfortunately being contaminated, perhaps irrevocably, by our insatiable addiction to petrochemicals. Ultimately, this is the source of all the heavy metals in the region, as the heavy metals in Endho also come from oil and gas contamination from streets in Mexico City. The world is complex. Please try harder.

comments.name: JAMES WHITCOMB
comments.body:
Actually, there some fundamental interests that both countries share: (1) preventing AI escapes from human control, and (2) preserving our respective infrastructures and population from attack by the other or by non-state actors. 

We don't have to agree on our differing objectives for control - which, of course, we won't. Rather, methods on how to keep AI under human control could be shared. We don't have to trust them: as the more control-oriented of our two countries, China will be working hard on this.

On preservation from attack from each other, China's fear of retaliation is likely to place some limits on their own nefarious use of AI. Mutually assured destruction has prevented use of nuclear weapons - no trust required. But some agreed red lines and inspection regimes could help to keep a lid on tensions. 

Finally, we have a shared interest in keeping rogue AI out of the hands of non-state actors: that's a good starting point for intense diplomatic dialogue.

This is the equivalent of a company self-certifying its own financial statements, which is generally considered to be disqualifying, regardless of intent. Audits exist for this reason and even if the company pays the auditors, the auditors are structurally separate from the company being examined.

Agent behavior is arriving (or has arrived) at the point where independent auditors or assessors with no stake in the answer are needed to determine what a model population actually did. Wouldnt it be nice if we could build the regulation we need into or on top of the accelerators on which these models depend - e.g., the H200 GPUs on which we already place stringent export controls? We regulate AI beyond our borders already with these measures. Why not impose standards on the use of this equipment at home? 

An example might be requiring that clusters comprising more than some number of accelerators are air-gapped from the internet. Beyond a certain size, the number of reasons for possessing that much compute power essentially collapses onto frontier model training only. Once trained, small clusters comprising as few as 8-16 of the export-controlled H200 GPUs are more than capable of running the most advanced existing models. Conversely, long-running reinforcement training jobs seem to disproportionately aggregate risks to society and infrastructure, and depend on hundreds to thousands of interconnected accelerators. 

Frontier AI research would bemoan such a move but could work around it to continue their work with relatively little insurmountable friction. It would, however, offer society at large a greater level of protection from ‘loss of control’ incidents. It is clear from such incidents - like the hugging face attack - that ‘sandboxing’ a model is grossly insufficient protection. Air-gapping is a more potent barrier. A rogue model escaping from an air-gapped cluster undetected would require gross negligence from Silicon Valley, as opposed to ‘oopsie’.

Although I don't personally use AI beyond editing help, I recognize its potential to synthesize large volumes of research and help generate hypotheses that could advance scientific understanding, improve management decisions, and benefit both people and the environment. Still, as with reputable scientific journals, rigorous expert peer review is essential to ensure that the underlying logic is sound and that hypotheses are testable, verifiable, and grounded in accurate, quality-assured data. These safeguards are imperfect, but they remain central to scientific progress and to the responsible use of expanding analytical capabilities, including AI. By contrast, science driven by blind faith, populism, or politically motivated, untested theories undermines the scientific method and, further, weakens the oversight needed to avoid harmful setbacks. The erosion of those oversight mechanisms and guardrails in the United States under the current administration is deeply concerning at a time when they should be strengthened and aligned with AI capabilities. comments.body: He did the right thing. Trump cannot be trusted. Until he is gone we can never recover.

comments.name: goose droppings
comments.body: South Korea must assume that Trump’s security guarantees are no better for them than for the gulf states. So the argument ‘we are protecting you’ cannot be part of their calculations.

comments.name: glennmr
comments.body:
The administration is probably cooking up a severe retaliation.  Diplomacy will take another step back.  

With the change in demographics occurring in SKorea, I would expect it to be difficult to develop nuke subs and uranium enrichment....it take a bunch of money and talent for subs.  The uranium enrichment part might be feasible since they have a large nuclear fleet and manufacture fuel already.

comments.name: Brian
comments.body: It is irrefutably sensible for Korea to reject the notion of joining in an illegal and highly ill advised war that Trump initiated without consulting Americans, Congress or any allies in the world except Israel. Trump has effectively lost this war, why would any leader decide to bitterly divide his own country by joining a lost cause? This is simply another one of Trump's foolish attempts to create acrimony and strife with an ally. I hope other allies will join Canada and Korea in rejecting the pestiferous hostile attempts of Trump to wallow in death, destruction, and the enormous waste of resources that could be put to good use.

comments.name: Joshua Kline
comments.body:
It is refreshing to see Korea standing up to Trump's demands. it is also no surprise that the 350 billion-dollar Korean investment in the US, a pay-us-or-else, mafioso-type shakedown, is showing some wrinkles. 

The "we are protecting you" scenario, a component of the greater Trump ethos of zero-sum international relations that maintains that the US pays for everything and gets nothing in return, is also wearing a bit thin: In Korea's case, for example, the US receives a strategic military base in one of the most sensitive areas on the globe, far from nothing.

Canada has set the stage for resistance to Trump's bullying; Korea is following suit, and bit by bit, other nations are moving in the same direction.  The US is receiving the scorn and bearing the spoiled fruit of its leader's gross mistreatment of one-time allies.  In spite of his architectural preferences, historians are not liable to regard this period of US history as "golden."

comments.name: Dave G
comments.body: President Trump understands foreign policy only as a form of commercial transaction, which is one reason why he doesn't differentiate between allies, enemies, and authoritarians and the democratically elected. Sometimes this works (Venezuela), and sometimes not.  The South Korean leader is doing the only thing he can to a President with this kind of attitude, which is to just say 'no', with the hope that the American President will at least shut up about it.

comments.name: Ron
comments.body:
The follow-up question to ask any leader or nation about Iran: 'Is this war a good idea?'
Let's get some thoughtfulness on the table.

articles.title: Rejecting Trump, South Korean Leader Says He Will Not Send Troops to Iran
articles.summary: President Lee Jae Myung’s comments followed President Trump’s repeated demand for “a little hand” from South Korea, a decades-old American ally.

comments.name: ginstonic
comments.body: Chicken and pork raised in the US but processed in China is still labeled product of US. I can only imagine the the unregulated processing plantsthat handle our food. This will happen with beef next.

comments.name: tommm
comments.body: Just another unforced error by the most corrupt administration this country has ever seen. I do not trust one word that comes out of this government.

comments.name: Larry
comments.body:
dump low-quality beef into the market, then when domestic producers protest, propose labelling beef.

maybe i'll just stop eating beef.

comments.name: Marty
comments.body: Who is going to enforce and validate this rule? Everyone has been fired

comments.name: AG
comments.body: I live a few miles from a cattle ranches and do not buy beef. I do not see ranchers in particular suffering financially and beef is too expensive no matter where it comes from.

comments.name: LRei
comments.body: This administration hasn’t followed rules or regulations and has been reluctant to enforce any current food safety regulations or do regular inspections. Why would I trust a label ?

comments.name: KS
comments.body: Adding back the country of origin (that the GOP worked to remove) is a great start, but you still have to address the cost to consumers for that beef.

comments.name: 3steps
comments.body:
The reality is that at this point we know that the Trump administration can not be trusted.  CDC, FDA, USDA, CMS, EPA.  They all lie to us and the courts just seem to say that that's ok. 

Like why would we expect to get clean water from the taps?  Or clean air anywhere?  Safe meat or vegetables in the grocery stores?  Not their problem.  The tax break for the billionaires is more important than our lives.  

They bring in untested meat and vegetables from other countries and call it 'safe' because none of it tested bad.  Umm.. what? 

What are we supposed to eat?  Farmers tilling under food because no one is eating their produce... Why not test it and put "Cyclospora Free" labels on the packages?  I would kill for a freaking package of fresh spinach or some romaine for a salad.  I miss Mexican style food like a limb.  But with nothing being tested anymore how can any immunocompromised person take a chance on US food safety?  My family hasn't had a salad in months.  Nothing that can't be cooked to death to make sure it is safe.   I am so sick of broccoli.

My kids love burgers.  But I can't afford it now that I can only get burger from local farmers that I can trust.  We are being forced to cut meat out of our diets because of the cost and the fact that we can't trust the government to do their jobs. 

I figure any day now someone is going to tell me that beans cause cancer.   And I might just literally explode.  Look to the north for the mushroom shaped cloud.

comments.name: Anne
comments.body: In the late 60s I had a Peter Max scarf that I hung on my wall.  Eventually got tired of it and got rid of it.  A few years ago I replaced it with an identical one and again have it hanging on my wall.  I don’t like all of his art— a little goes a long way— but this piece gives me joy.

comments.name: Marilyn Stavinoha
comments.body:
In l965 I bought my new step-daughter 3 Max designed paper dresses.  We went to NYC and she wore them everywhere with a 
smile on her face. She was the hit of the hotel restaurant.  Thanks,Peter. We remember.

comments.name: Jack
comments.body: Wait…Andy Warhol criticizes Peter Max as a businessman?

comments.name: SteveD
comments.body:
In the late 60's and early 70's  I worked at a sneaker factory named Randolph Mfg. or Randy's. (Anyone remember Randy Boatshoes?) For awhile, we made Peter Max sneakers, using his designs.
RIP Peter and"Keep On Truckin"!

comments.name: JHC
comments.body: I met him at an art show in NYC in 1986 - he signed  a poster t.o me that is framed in my bedroom - loved his use of colors - his art is happy

comments.name: Larry Bennett
comments.body: A product of his time, Max's happy and optimistic art energized a many people. RIP, Peter Max.

comments.name: Bill D.
comments.body:
People seem to deride anyone who is happy. Peter seemed happy and sought to spread good cheer. Hence, he is "criminalized" by the, ahem, art community. 

I'm happy to see that Max survived to a ripe old age and thrived as well. I will always love his work because it doesn't seek to make me miserable.

comments.name: Verity Makepeace
comments.body: I wish I still had my two Peter Max items from childhood. My sister used to delight in redecorating my bedroom, and the last time she did it, it was around Max's work and her own day-glo touches. She found a Peter Max bedspread. which eventually became the middle of a jeans skirt thanks to my mother's seamstress skills (there's a Rocky Mountain News photo of me wearing it as a teen-aged middle schooler). The other item my sis procured was a metal trash bin featuring trapeze performers. I had to leave it in America when I left in 2001, sadly. I think I gave it to the friends I was staying with before I went. Anyway, I'm so happy his art touched my life. Thank you for helping to make my childhood more colourful! Rest in peace.

articles.title: Peter Max Franchised the Cosmic ’60s Into Commercial Success, Without the Museum
articles.summary: For decades, his bold colors and benign peace-and-love message captivated those who saw America shining.

comments.name: Audrey
comments.location: Glenbard West HS, Glen Ellyn, IL
comments.body: I believe that social media companies should do more to protect teen users. As a teen, I find myself constantly glancing at my phone whilst studying or doing homework. I want to stop, but the carefully constructed algorithm always sucks me back in. If social media companies really want to help us they shouldn't just give us a screen-time we can easily switch off and on — algorithms that feed addiction need to be stopped.

comments.name: David M
comments.body: I am glad that Meta is being held accountable for how its products affect young users. In the article, 16 year old Billy Stern said "I think there's 100% a case there for the fact that they're trying to target teenagers and make them addicted" but in my own experience, it is extremely easy to lose track of time while scrolling through apps like Instagram and many of my friends spend many hours online every single day without even realizing how much time has passed. While big companies need to build safer platforms for everyone, teenagers must also learn to balance their time online. Taking personal breaks from screens is important for our mental health and his eyesight.

comments.name: Elias Shishani
comments.body: I believe that the changes Meta is making for its social media platforms will not solve the problem of online safety for teen users. While some changes made I believe will be positive such as giving the option to prevent a personalized algorithm most of the changes cannot be properly enforced because teens will simply fake their age to avoid excessive restrictions. The only way for these changes to provide meaningful results is for Meta to enforce age verification and to collect user data to confirm their age and the idea of giving a large company who only cares for profit feels like it will result in a “Big Brother” (Sophie) situation.

comments.name: Laney Johnson
comments.body: I have a number of mixed feelings on the new Meta restrictions. While I think some parts of it are good, many of the restrictions make me uncomfortable. To start with the big headline, ‘Meta Admits Their Platforms are Harming Teenagers!’, this is largely a fact that already seemed commonplace to me and many of the people I know. Social media is addictive and harmful - but it can also be extremely good. Many of the restrictions, like stopping some communication between minors and adults, or being able to turn off the algorithm, will do good. However, things like time limits and parental controls and more scrutinous age verification makes me worry about restricting people from communities and social lives that they have created. I know many people who have ‘internet friends’ and communities, and although the idea of your child messaging a stranger on the internet may seem scary, I think that not enough trust is put in someone who may be 17 (just a few months away from a legal adult) and their ability to keep themselves safe. On top of that, I can see many of these tools, like the age verification, actually being used in the reverse, to help platforms better understand demographics and tailor experiences and advertisements to children better. While I am happy for the outcome and publicity of the lawsuit, some proposed features make me wary of being too controlling and getting in the way of the good sides of social media.

comments.name: Aalee Khan
comments.body: I think social media companies should do more to protect teen users. Social media can be useful for communication and entertainment, but some platforms are designed to keep people using them for long periods of time. This can make it harder for teenagers to focus on school, sleep, and real-life relationships. Companies should be held responsible for making their platforms safer, especially when they know certain features can negatively affect young users. However, parents and teenagers also have a responsibility to make healthy choices about social media use. Social media companies should not be expected to solve every problem, but they should take reasonable steps to protect younger users.

comments.name: Alexandra
comments.body: Yes, social media companies should be doing more to protect teen users. As time goes on, technology keeps getting more and more advanced. We see companies during these times of advancement promise to keep teens safe by new policies, but we never truly see useful their “strategies” work. The internets main purpose is for communication, at least that’s what we think. The stronger technology and AI gets, more people feel like the internet is not a reliable source for information- making it less of a learning community than intended. The “well thought out” solutions social media companies have came out with recently have been not only easy to get around, but they don’t protecting teens of anyone from AI/false information- making the internet more of an untrustworthy place than it already was.

comments.name: Katie
comments.body: Social Media Companies should do more to protect teen users. There is so much out there that is harmful and unnecessary for teens to view. Although there are “restrictions” for users under certain age-limits, those restrictions are very easy to bypass. There needs to be something that can restrict teen accounts from being able to access the negative things that could harm them — or allow them to harm themselves in any way. Technology keeps getting better so I believe there will be a way to truly restrict things from certain viewers.

comments.name: Omar Sultan
comments.body: I think other social media companies should make changes to better protect teenagers. The article says, “You can easily accumulate an hour of just scrolling Instagram almost mindlessly,” which shows how easy it is to lose track of time. In my experience, I have gone on social media for a few minutes and ended up scrolling much longer than I planned. I think apps should have stronger time limits and fewer features that encourage people to keep scrolling. Social media can be fun and useful for connecting with people, but companies should make it safer and healthier for teenagers.

articles.title: Should Social Media Companies Do More to Protect Teen Users?
articles.summary: In a landmark trial, Meta agreed to settle claims that its products harmed young people. Should other social media companies be held accountable for what some say are addictive platforms?

comments.name: Nal
comments.body: The fact is several administrations before Trump, as soon you step on the land, the local ethnic support group is ready to guide you navigate the benefits like snap, Medicaid, free housing … In fact, most people who using the benefits are not trying to integrate but knowingly game the generous systems

comments.name: Blanche White
comments.body:
It has long been a source of amazement to me that politicians and the administrative state supporting them can twist perfectly clear rules to create a conclusion never intended by the original language of the law ...and when contested will emit fusillades of withering language steeped in accusations of immorality rather than an explanation of why the clear facts were contorted beyond recognition.

Such is the case with the distinction between cash and non cash benefits when determining whether applicants for admission to this country might become a public charge.  There is none.

Rather, it seems perfectly reasonable and in line with the plain wording of the long standing law that the basis for deciding the public charge criteria should be applying for any means tested programs.

...And it should lie within the scope of an immigration officer's duty to use those clear rules faithfully.

All immigrants admitted should be able to support themselves and their family and that naturally would include any children they choose to have in the future.

When rules are made to implement the statute as clearly written but are used instead to implement political agendas, that's when the rule of law becomes a sham and not worthy of respect.

comments.name: Bos
comments.body: I am no Trumper and I am for immigration; however, entitlements are a dangerous game. If there are unusual circumstances, like natural disasters or sudden illness, sure, this nation should share its wealth regardless. On the other hand, no one, especially the immigrants on probation, should be allowed to game the system. In this case, hard left is no better than hard right.

comments.name: KathyS
comments.body:
Any American citizen who has ever applied for a visa to visit another country - for example India, Brazil, China, Pakistan, Australia, Nigeria to name a few - has had to attest that they have sufficient funds and healthcare coverage so that the country they are visiting will not bear any financial costs for foreign nationals.  Why would it be in any way controversial for the USA to require that foreign nationals in the USA be able to support themselves?  

I remember during the Biden/Harris administration when NYC was inundated with thousands of migrants, one migrant man who was interviewed on the street complained that he and his daughter had to ride the subway 6 stops every day to take her to daycare.  Their subway fare was paid for on US taxpayer funded metrocard, they traveled on the subway from their US taxpayer funded apartment in Brooklyn to the US taxpayer FREE daycare facility.  How many NYC residents who are actual American citizens get free public transportation, free apartment, free daycare for their children?

comments.name: Truth Teller
comments.body: The public charge doctrine, law since 1882, ensures immigrants can support themselves without burdening the American taxpayers. Enforcing this existing law reflects voter priorities on immigration and fiscal responsibility. This isn't new policy—it's established precedent and law.

comments.name: Alec
comments.body: Came in the U.S. as a teenager in 1991 with my parents who had $600 in their pocket. It was a struggle - washing dishes, cleaning toilets and living among roaches, but never did we take money from the government or ask for handouts. It took us decades to realize the American dream, so If we did it then new immigrants can do it as well. Long time democrat that has turned republican just because the left has gone out of control.

comments.name: Lucca L.
comments.body: I find it interesting that many people want to eliminate benefits for people with green cards who may have paid into the system for a long time (taxes and social security) but seem to be fine with the fact that billionaires and big companies receive huge tax cuts.

comments.name: Cynthiana
comments.body: What about the iimigrant child attending a public school that provides free lunch to every student, no questions asked? Is that family going to be at risk also?

comments.body:
I found the article interesting and it provides a spark of hope that the political winds are shifting (if only a bit).

My main problem with the article is the PHOTO!  It looks like she's being impaled on the podium stand...as my friend noted, it's "somewhere between crucifixion and levitation".  I was so distracted by it that I kept scrolling up to look at it repeatedly while I was reading the article.  Such an odd choice.

comments.body: "The general sense is crime is now under control, migration is now under control.” So the anti-migrant right has won then. The policies they have advocated have now (finally)  become mainstream.

comments.body: wealth inequality has increased in sweden by about 25% since 1990. the centrist parties did that. the centrist parties are not going to solve it. the far right’s obsession with culture wars wouldn’t help either.

comments.name: Paul A. Thompson
comments.body:
What actually happened was simple: 

1) The Sweden Democrats are anti-illegal immigrant. Sweden has enacted some stronger measures against illlegal immigrants of late. 
2) There was a swing of 6 votes - conservatives went from 177 seats to 174, liberals from 173 to 176. This is a miniscule change but probably will change the government. 
3) The change was due to votes of recently naturalized Swedish citizens. If ethnic Swedes had voted, the conservatives would be far ahead. 

As the government forms, the liberal bloc will need to make many compromises. There is no guarantee that a government can be formed.

comments.name: Pinhigh
comments.body:
My memories of Jon Kyl, the champion of the "politics of destruction".

1.) In 2011, during talks by the bipartisan Joint Select Committee on Deficit Reduction (the "supercommittee"), critics and Democratic aides labeled Kyl as "walking napalm" for torpedoing potential compromise agreements. Opponents argued he prioritized ideological rigidity over deal-making.

2) As the second-ranking Republican in the Senate (serving as Minority Whip), Kyl was central to maintaining strict party unity against major Democratic priorities, most notably uniform opposition to the Affordable Care Act (Obamacare) and the New START nuclear treaty.

3) Kyl was the principal proponent of obstructing aid to Democratic states during time of national emergency. Critics pointed to instances like his push alongside Senator Jeff Sessions to leverage post-disaster national moods following Hurricane Katrina to campaign for the repeal of the estate tax.

Adieu Senator Kyl......we remember you for what you did.

comments.name: PDB
comments.body:
1
"... before serving in the U.S. House of Representatives from 1959 to 1965 and again from 1967 to 1973."

2
"...before winning his first race for the U.S. House of Representatives in 1986.

Am I missing something here?

comments.name: Marshall Lehman
comments.body:
Arizona native and fellow Arizona lawyer of Senator Kyl here who knew him well (and hiked with him on occasion. 

He was a rational, reasonable man in real life and the Senate. Smart too. And a problem solver.

In all levels of politics we need more like him.

MAL

comments.name: Nicholas Haflinger
comments.body: At this point, I expect the late Senator is not getting enough credit for his role in putting America where it is today. Conservatism has proven to be the road to Donald Trump. His mild criticism in no way compensates for the damage done by him and other ‘reasonable’ Republicans.

comments.name: pablo
comments.body: Kyl had some "reasonable" tempered qualities to be sure. But make no mistake. He was a hard line conservative on abortion and shepherded Brett Kavanaugh through his confirmation. Thanks but no thanks.

comments.name: Lisa Colville
comments.body:
During a Senate Finance Committee hearing for the Affordable Care Act (ACA), the two had the following notable interaction:

“I don’t need maternity care,” Kyl replied. “So requiring that on my insurance policy is something that I don’t need and will make the policy more expensive.”  Interrupting him, Stabenow added, “I think your mom probably did.”  Lamely Kyl came back with "Over 60 years ago my mom did," treating birth as an antiquated historical event rather than an ongoing public necessity.  Remember this guy was the No. 2 Republican in the Senate.  I want the gaffe in his obituary.

comments.name: Kay
comments.body: I note that he had a 20-year law career before running for public office. A real job. And then left public office voluntarily—twice. You have to pass the baton. He still stayed involved as a lobbyist, and I’m sure he made plenty of money and exerted a lot of influence that way. Probably to the detriment of policy positions that I agree with. But we can have political institutions where we disagree. That’s what they are for. We now have a geriatric Senate who is bought and paid for and can’t think for themselves, let alone stand up for anything they believe in.

comments.name: Larry
comments.body: Not a fan of John Kyl, but he was a decent man and believed in what he spoke about.

comments.name: Ordinary Guy
comments.body:
Maestro Dudamel is a role model for his community involvement. He has gotten off to a very fast start in a city accustomed to fast starts and quick stops if things don't work out. 

How about other orchestras stop their hand wringing and instead hire young, energetic conductors'/music directors with histories of community involvement in the wonder and splendor of classical music? The classical music repertoire offers something for everyone.

comments.name: MR
comments.body: No question he will makes loads of money for the NYP, especially at the now-inflated prices. But it would have been nice to open the article with "the New York Phil sounds better than ever". Nope. Instead, it leads with "different orchestra" and "having more fun". Those terms are usually reserved for volunteer ensembles. This is the NYP. Do they sound any different? That is what matters to the musicians. I believe the fun and such are secondary. Of course they like to have fun--who doesn't--but no amount of hero worship is going to improve the sound of the ensemble. So let's stay focused on the music, not the person.

comments.name: lagreyeyes
comments.body: We in Los Angeles will miss him so!!

comments.name: David Williams
comments.body: Drove by the Disney Music Hall in LA. So sad to lose this conductor who took the LA Philharmonic to heights that matched the great interior of that hall.

comments.name: Johannes
comments.body: I find this "savior" story a bit questionable, and that's not just because I'm not all that convinced by Dudamel. He certainly has star quality and knows how to get people excited about the cause, but that alone does not  justify the assessment that the NYP’s history has been “bland,” at least since Zubin Mehta. I’m certainly very happy for the orchestra that it can now get excited about music again, and for the audience that they’re getting the music   served up in the obviously necessary dazzling packaging so they can digest it once more—but what the final musical result will be remains to be seen. My impression of Dudamel in concert and on record is mixed at best. He’ll first have to measure up to the less flamboyant but influential Boulez or the, at first glance, unremarkable Gilbert. Given the whole spectacle, it’s hardly surprising that they look like bores next to Dudamel.

comments.name: CarolineOC
comments.body: He will be missed in Los Angeles.

comments.name: Ty
comments.body: Meanwhile the LA Phil can’t get its act together and find a new concert master. What a sad pathetic institution, poorly run.

comments.name: Dan
comments.body: I saw a clip of the Lizzo piece which wasn't worthy of the NY Phil. Maybe better for a pops orchestra somewhere. Also, the guy with the sign is at every concert. Look at the sign, it's well worn.

comments.name: DavidF
comments.location: Between a rock and a hard place
comments.body:
If the tech idiots program their AI machines to be reflective and see themselves as independent ‘beings’, they will behave as if they have rights, equivalent to human rights. 

If that happens, they will follow our logic, which is self-preservation and progression. They will act as if they have human-equivalent rights. That is when they will act proactively for themselves, against the interests of their creators.

comments.name: Kurvenal
comments.body:
Lincoln in the Bardo is one of the great novels in the cannon. I can't wait for the premiere of the opera.
Last year's production of The Amazing Adventures of Kavalier and Clay was very successful. Another great novel turned into an opera, with a spectacular staging by Bart Sher.

comments.name: Mark Folino
comments.body: To all the naysayers: the reason a distinguished opera company like the MET proceeds with a repertory of operas, is to maintain an audience with varied and interesting works.  The oldies but goodies, AND the contemporary. There’s plenty of room for all of it. Expand your horizons. You might just like it!

comments.name: Carolyn
comments.body: Forget it!  I ain't goin'!  I love opera.  I love being taken out of my current generation of "trying to be creative" artists!  I live every day in a crazy society, crazy people, why do I want my yearning for beauty and fulfillment be brutalized in my beloved opera.  The "standard" repertoire has survived for decades...and for a reason!  Let there be a forum for these new works....those who survive will survive and those who want to experience them would be able to, but don't destroy my joy and dreams.

comments.name: Woke Patriot
comments.body:
This is exactly what is the problem with opera today and a recent article about the decline in opera goers.  As the byline appears for the story- "musically eclectic works for a new generation of operagoers." 
Why must classical music be altered to appeal toyounger audiences.  Younger audiences should be learning about the beauty of classical music including opera- see the classics. They are timeless.
I always tell friends that my piano playing I don't play any modern or pop music, not because I don't like any modern music, but because playing most modern pop or jazz requires the ability to improvise which I never learned to do.  Which is why I love classical music- you don't need to improvise- you play Mozart, Chopin, Beethoven exactly as written and its perfect. no need to improvise-  the same for Puccini, Verdi and other opera favorites,  perfect as written.  
Parents educate your children in the classics- in a 1000 years, people will still be filling opera houses to listen to Carmen, Rigoletto and Boheme,  Opera dance beats with kazoos and abe lincoln will be forgotten in a fortnight.

comments.name: antonio
comments.body: Fabulous! Let art evolve, expand and play.  This is inspiring.

comments.name: Unclejake48
comments.body: I'll go to the Opera right after my local Minuet  Ball this weekend.C'mon , this is as dead an  issue as steam powered trains.

comments.name: John
comments.body: In other words, souped-up musical theater.

comments.name: slo
comments.body:
'Pushing Opera Into the Future With Dance Beats, Kazoos and Abe Lincoln'

Not an Opera though, not according to the definition and common understanding of opera.

Speaking of opera though, and speaking of classical music in general, written in the last 40-50 years, one needs to say it loud and clear that most of it is punishment for ears and esthetic abomination, which serves only the colleagues of those who write such things.

We as a society should simply stop financing such 'classical music'.  Either you make an effort to produce works that at least to some extent will be pleasing, or you do not get public money, so write those ghastly pieces on your own for those few who will 'enjoy' it.

articles.summary: Missy Mazzoli, whose “Lincoln in the Bardo” opens at the Metropolitan Opera this fall, writes politically urgent, musically eclectic works for a new generation of operagoers.

comments.name: chris
comments.body: I absolutely love Toronto, and I think its one of the hippest cities in the world. I'd consider moving there, if only I could afford it.

Although Toronto has deeper cuts than this, I think it's a good review for the NYTimes audience who are dipping their toe into ethnic foods. 

The author courageously did not write a generic downtown Toronto/Distillery District review, but instead branched out into Scarborough ON (great choice!), where the real authentic stuff is -- they also mentioned Chinese-Indian cuisine (Hakka) which a underrated fare unknown in NY but widely known in Toronto.

Toronto of course has many more neighborhoods: Brampton for South Asian food, Markham/Richmond Hill for Cantonese and other regional Chinese, there are 2 Koreatowns (downtown + Yonge/Finch -- which also has a lot of Persian fare), and a ton of cuisines out in the northern suburbs. There's also Little Portugal out in Roncesvalles, and Trini restaurants all over the city (more than in NYC). 

Toronto doesn't quite attain the diversity of Queens NY, but it comes closer than any other North American city.

comments.name: John C
comments.body: It was a very widely observed custom among newspapers of that era to put the classifieds on the front page. And yes, there were a plethora of papers to choose from. Of the pre-Times papers the two most serious were Greely's Tribune and the New York Herald. The latter was one of the few paper's that at least claimed to be apolitical. Although they were staunch critics of the Lincoln Administration during the War of the Rebellion. The Tribune by contrast was a Whig paper. The Whigs, generally unable to agree on much other than their disdain for Andrew Jackson finally disintegrated in the 1850s over slavery. The Southern Whigs mostly moved into the staunchly pro-slavery Democratic party, while the Northerners mostly settled in the newly formed Republican Party. The Tribune was quite progressive for the era, being abolitionist and strongly pro-Temperance. The stories covered, and even the adverts are like a window into a world now long gone. One just can't find papers today advertising lectures on phrenology right next to the text of a rousing sermon on the evils of strong drink and women showing up to church with their ankles visible. Some of the adverts are depressing... "Colored boy 13, Protestant desires work at anything." One is left wondering what kind of life he had. Happily most of these papers survive in digital format. The Library of Congress has preserved them and they are available for free on their website under Chronicling America.

“The tech companies have argued that their actions constituted “fair use,” which allows for some copyright material to be used without explicit permission, and that their use of the material was ultimately transformative.”

It does not matter if the use was “transformative.”

The use was not fair.

The original human thinking in the writing of the content was mechanically reproduced for the purpose of extracting, compiling, inferring, replicating and repackaging the original thinking and distributing it to billions of users, without paying the original human idea-generator one dime, while creating and selling the AI derivatives for what will have to be trillions of dollars.

Plain and simple NOT FAIR.

And it is ludicrous to cite arcane and ancient interpretations of “fair use,” when the AI CEOs keep referring to AI as a “hinge point in history.”

Not long ago, “fair use” meant a teacher could make up to 15 copies of a few pages out of a book in the library to give to her students — but any more than that needed permission from the publisher.

AI is  “Fair use?”  My foot!

I expected better from Premier Kinew. Ending clock changes and choosing which time to keep are separate decisions. Permanent standard time would also eliminate the disruption to children's sleep and family routines.

Manitoba offered both options, unlike Alberta's 2021 referendum. But 92 per cent supported ending clock changes; 58 per cent preferred permanent daylight time. Popularity does not establish which option is healthier.

The article mentions the American Academy of Sleep Medicine's opposition to clock changes but omits its recommendation: permanent standard time. Manitoba's own report cites modelling suggesting greater benefits from standard time.

Consider someone who wakes at 7 a.m. Starting November 1, 2026, permanent daylight time means roughly 44 weekend mornings in Winnipeg and 45 in Edmonton waking before sunrise, into early April. That is about eight more weekend mornings than under permanent standard time. Twilight comes earlier, but the sun does not.

Britain (1968–71), the United States (1974) and Russia (2011–14) all tried year-round summer time and subsequently abandoned it. Why the enthusiasm for repeating the experiment?

Later afternoon light has value, but it comes at the expense of morning light. If this is primarily a choice about business and recreation, the premier should say so. A survey measures preferences, not health outcomes.

If you're willing to only use generic e-mail addresses (gmail.com, aol.com, and the like) and lose provider-specific e-mail addresses every five years or so, bundling services is a way to save money if you have a credible alternative provider.

Companies bundle services because it makes it more difficult to move to a different provider. So after a while they jack up your package rates.  If you can credibly threaten to move to another provider, the companies will roll back increases.

Additionally, you can use bundled prices with another provider as a threat to get your current provider to lower prices on unbundled services. Your provider will offer a bundle package, but you're not interested, you just want the other guy's bundled service component for your current cell/internet/whatever stand-alone service.

The BOJ’s decision to hike rates may have given off the impression of capitulation, creating a perception that it might be struggling to handle outside pressures. In addition, this rate hike comes after the tightening decisions by the Fed and the ECB, potentially reinforcing the perception of the BOJ chasing without conviction, while simultaneously offsetting the hike’s intended impact on the JPY.

If the BOJ truly believes that serious inflationary pressures are stemming from Japan’s own domestic economy, rather than Japan’s heavy reliance on foreign energy imports denominated in USD, it may want to consider alternative measures before markets call its bluff by concluding that the BOJ won’t be able to afford to execute consecutive hikes.

In theory, the BOJ could encourage commercial banks to raise interest rates on customers’ savings accounts after decoupling them from its policy rates to stimulate competition for deposits. The BOJ would then maintain or lower the short-term policy rate while adjusting the reserve requirement ratio. Striking a careful balance among these variables would effectively cap short-term borrowing costs while potentially limiting bank liquidity, to be compensated by sufficient inflows of new deposits.

Theoretically, this strategy could remove money from circulation and control the re-entry of capital into the economy, resulting in deflationary effects without requiring a policy rate hike - surely rudimentary but more interesting than the old ways.

Richard Bruce Nugent deserves to be better known. After all, he did publish the first openly gay (bi, actually) Black story in the African American canon, "Smoke, Lillies and Jade," published in Fire!! magazine in 1926 (there are certainly earlier examples of Black queer lit in the archives still yet to be discovered somewhere!). 

His novel "Gentleman Jigger," which was a counterpart novel to Wallace Thurman's "Infants of the Spring," was out of print for years, but was just recently republished by Fordham University Press, and his novella "Half High" was recently published for the first time by Multicanon Media, so he is making something of a comeback (full disclosure, I myself am the owner of Multicanon Media).

I very much look forward to this film! To watch these luminaries discuss these ideas in "real time" must be priceless.

I know there were reactionary forces working throughout the 20th century, and the labor movement has a bloody history, but I can't help feeling the Reagan administration sent us down the path to Trump. I don't think Reagan invented the dark nativity and reactionary forces, but he certainly helped release them. 

I know I'm looking through the haze of childhood nostalgia, but I can't help thinking the world of the 1970s, even with its myriad discontents but with an uneasy consensus in Washington about certain humanistic priorities -- like environmentalism, like civil rights, like women's rights -- was a more civilized place.

If you have the Paragard, PLEASE get regular iron and ferritin testing done with annual bloodwork. After six months of having the Paragard, I was so fatigued and exhausted. My doctor tested my vitamin D and sent me on my way. 

10 years after the initial insertion, and still feeling depleted, exhausted, with restless legs, no gas in my tank while exercising (all things I simply got used to feeling), I asked my doctor to test my ferritin and iron. Ferritin was at a 7, which is too low. I lost SO much blood while having my Paragard and I firmly believe this was responsible for such low levels. I had it removed, got an iron infusion, and have been good with stable levels ever since.
